title: Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
abstract: Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses . Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware. Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware. Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware. It boots the same system images as real hardware and runs a realistic software stack against virtual hardware. This enables Cuttlefish to more closely track a physical device’s behavior than a lightweight emulator does. Unfortunately, Cuttlefish is only supported on Linux, and our application and library developers work on Macs with Apple silicon. This forced us to support Goldfish and Cuttlefish side by side. We knew if we could consolidate onto a single Cuttlefish-based platform, we could give all of our developers the benefit of the same high-fidelity virtual device. The challenge was porting the stack to make Cuttlefish run natively on macOS. The Impact of Fragmentation Maintaining dual emulator platforms imposed a heavy operational burden: It drained computing resources, created confusion for developers, and slowed down the emulator team. Every tool required support for two separate platforms, while infrastructure and engineering capacity were divided between them. Furthermore, developers had to choose an emulator target based on how they worked: Goldfish ran everywhere but had less fidelity while Cuttlefish needed Linux. The AOSP mirrors this exact divide: Goldfish targets application developers, whereas Cuttlefish serves Android platform developers. So long as we maintained that division, we would suffer the effects of fragmentation. The Stack and the macOS Gaps Cuttlefish is the orchestration layer, while the component that actually runs the guest OS is a virtual machine monitor (VMM). On Linux, Cuttlefish normally uses crosvm but previously included support for QEMU as an alternative VMM. That integration had become inactive over time . To enable native Apple silicon support on macOS, we revived QEMU support. Many of Cuttlefish’s virtual devices use vhost-user backends, separate processes that provide virtio devices to QEMU over a socket. The architecture is clean, but large parts of it were written with a hard Linux assumption. Three of those assumptions break on macOS. The vhost-user machinery is gated to Linux and won’t build or run. The Apple hypervisor imposes resource limits QEMU didn’t expect. Finally, the native display, build, and signing paths didn’t exist. We tackled all three. The Cuttlefish-on-Mac stack. Cuttlefish orchestrates virtual devices backed by QEMU. The highlighted orange blocks are the Mac-specific work: adding macOS support to vhost-user, increasing memory-region tracking slots in QEMU’s HVF backend, and using the native Cocoa display and code-signing paths. Making vhost-user Portable Beyond Linux The most structurally important changes were in QEMU’s vhost-user path. The frontends, libvhost-user , and the contrib backends such as vhost-user-blk were all gated to Linux. We relaxed those build restrictions so the vhost-user frontends and libraries can build on macOS as well as Linux. This lets Cuttlefish’s device backends hand off to QEMU on a Mac the same way they do on Linux. Without this, the higher-fidelity device model that makes Cuttlefish worth using isn’t available outside Linux. title: Production MLOps at GS Caltex with Amazon SageMaker Canvas, part 1
abstract: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. Solution overview The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. From a validated model to a repeatable workflow You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
abstract: Coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI work in tasks. A developer asks for a change, and the agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests until the work is done. One task can take a few model calls or dozens. What the developer pays for is the task, not one call. The price per token alone doesn’t tell you what a whole task costs. The total depends on how many turns a model needs, how much history each turn replays, and how often a task has to be retried or never finishes. You pay for every attempt, including attempts on tasks that never finish. So when you route a coding agent’s requests between models, judge the routing by cost per solved task: the total cost of your runs divided by the number of runs whose tests pass. NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard is an open source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. You define the models that it can use and the strategy that it follows. Its LiteLLM integration supports two strategies. Stage routing reads the recent tool activity and results in the request history, and then picks one of two candidate models. Random routing picks from the configured models, with optional weights, for traffic splits and A/B comparisons. Another option you can explore is LiteLLM, who also recently shipped a native built-in Switchyard stage router as an auto-router strategy. In this post, you use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy LiteLLM, an open source gateway for large language models (LLMs), with the Switchyard routing plugin in your AWS account. LiteLLM calls the models on Amazon Bedrock . You then use the sample’s benchmark runners to measure cost per solved task for a routed model group and for single-model baseline groups, so that you can evaluate routing against your own workloads. Note: The sample installs switchyard-server 0.3.0 from crates.io and runs the published LiteLLM v1.102.0 image. NVIDIA documents switchyard-server 0.3.0 as a demo and evaluation component, and its configuration can change between releases. This sample uses the experimental Switchyard LiteLLM integration and its configuration and APIs may change between releases. This is sample code, for non-production usage. Work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before deployment. Deploy the sample in a non-production account and test it before relying on it. Solution overview Figure 1 shows the architecture of the solution. LiteLLM and the Switchyard plugin run in one container image on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate , in private subnets. Figure 1: Solution architecture A request flows through these steps. The numbers match the diagram. The coding agent sends an OpenAI-compatible request with the model field set to switchyard , the LiteLLM model group that Switchyard routes, and the shared gateway key in the Authorization header. The endpoint is your hostname over HTTPS, with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate on the load balancer, and only the IPv4 CIDR range that you allow can reach it. With a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53 , Route 53 resolves the hostname to the load balancer. AWS WAF filters the request with IP reputation, known bad input, and per-IP rate-limit rules. The Application Load Balancer forwards only /v1/chat/completions , /v1/models , and /health/liveliness to the ECS task in a private subnet, and answers every other path with 404. The task runs one container: LiteLLM with the embedded Switchyard plugin. LiteLLM validates the gateway key and calls the plugin to pick a model. Stage chooses between a capable model and a lower-cost efficient model. It reads the tool activity and results in the request history, so the agent must send the full conversation history. title: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
abstract: Agents today review code, process claims, and run unattended for hours. Many also sit behind interactive experiences where a person waits for the first response. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime gives these agents a fully managed, serverless environment: each session runs in its own isolated microVM, the platform scales to zero when there’s no work, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume. AgentCore runtime with platformVersion set to “V2” changes how sessions start. Instead of initializing your container for every session, it prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores that snapshot for each new session. Session start times are faster and more consistent. V2 also reclaims memory your sessions don’t use, so your bill tracks what your agent uses. For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes. Some agents need restructuring to get the full benefit, and for chat and voice experiences even 2 seconds is too slow. This post explains how V2 starts a session, how to measure session start time, and how to keep work off the first request, including build hooks, which AgentCore runtime now supports. We cover four patterns, from changes to your agent’s code to starting sessions before users need them. Which pattern do you need? Your situation What to do Section A new session in about 2 seconds is fine Switch to V2 and do all initialization before app.run() Keep work off the first request Your agent needs large files, a CLI, or a browser early, and can’t hold them in its process Add a build hook to load and prime them while the snapshot is built Working with hooks You need sub-second, and users engage before they send their first request (opening the app or a chat window) Start the session in the background when the user engages Pre-warm on user engagement How V2 starts a session AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM. On V1, AgentCore pulls your container image from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), starts the container, and runs your initialization code before it can process the first request. The image pull dominates, so cold start grows with image size. V2 does that work once. When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore runtime starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping ( GET /ping ), which must arrive within 120 seconds. It then clears the operating system’s file cache, to keep the snapshot small, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot. This is a change from V1: Every create or update now takes a few minutes while the snapshot is built. In this post, init means everything your agent does before /ping reports healthy. With the AgentCore Python SDK, that’s everything before app.run() . If you run your own HTTP server, in Node.js or another language, report healthy only after your initialization finishes. Figure 1: Build, once per create or update When a new session arrives, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM. Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with its imports, objects, and clients in place. Files from your image are loaded lazily: each block is fetched the first time a session reads it. Figure 2: Invoke, every new session Three facts follow from these flows, and the rest of this post builds on them: Memory comes back whole. Anything your process held at snapshot time, and anything in a RAM-backed file system such as /dev/shm , is available at memory speed from the first access. File reads don’t carry over. The file cache is cleared before the freeze, so reading a file during init doesn’t make it fast in a restored session. Image files are fetched on first read. The first read of a block comes from snapshot storage and is then cached closer to the host. title: OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures
abstract: You can deploy OpenFold3-preview from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . The OpenFold Consortium and the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University developed OpenFold3 as an open source biomolecular structure prediction model. With a few lines of code, you can typically deploy OpenFold3 into your own AWS account. You can then predict the 3D structures of proteins, DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, and the complexes they form. The endpoint runs with network isolation, which you can use to help keep your sequences within your AWS account. Computational drug discovery teams now use structure prediction as a core part of their work. Teams use it in target identification, antibody and protein engineering, and structure-based virtual screening. Teams have found running these models challenging. You need GPU infrastructure, a working CUDA and PyTorch stack, large model checkpoints, and a serving layer that handles requests that take minutes rather than milliseconds. SageMaker JumpStart can handle much of that work for you. OpenFold3 runs in an AWS-maintained container on a managed Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint. The endpoint is designed to handle request queuing and GPU warmup, and you can add autoscaling. In this post, we show you how to: Deploy OpenFold3-preview on a SageMaker asynchronous inference endpoint. Submit structure prediction jobs and interpret the results, including predicted structures and confidence scores. Run several predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances . Supply your own multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to improve prediction accuracy while helping keep your sequences private. Help reduce costs by scaling your endpoint to zero when it’s idle. Overview of OpenFold3 OpenFold3 is an all-atom structure prediction model. It predicts the joint 3D structure of a set of molecules from their sequences. It isn’t limited to single protein chains: It can fold multi-chain protein complexes, protein–nucleic acid assemblies, and protein–ligand complexes in one prediction. Attribute Details Developer OpenFold Consortium / AlQuraishi Lab, Columbia University Model type All-atom biomolecular structure prediction Inputs Protein, DNA, and RNA sequences. Small-molecule ligands as SMILES Outputs Predicted structures in mmCIF format, with confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, PDE) Version OpenFold3 0.4.1, of3-p2-155k checkpoint License Apache 2.0 JumpStart model ID huggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3 Supported instances ml.g6.2xlarge , ml.g6.4xlarge (default), ml.g6.12xlarge The OpenFold3 developers release its code and model weights under the Apache 2.0 license, and they publish the training data and methods. Research organizations and pharmaceutical companies can inspect the model, fine-tune it, and build on it under the terms of that license. The developers describe OpenFold3-preview as a research preview. Use cases Target and complex structure prediction – Predict structures for targets that have no experimental structure, including multi-chain assemblies and protein–nucleic acid complexes. Protein–ligand co-folding – Fold a protein together with a small molecule supplied as SMILES to generate binding-pose hypotheses for structure-based design. Antibody and protein engineering – Evaluate designed variants by predicting their structures and comparing confidence across candidates. High-throughput screening pipelines – Queue large batches of prediction jobs against an autoscaling endpoint and process the results directly from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A real-time endpoint returns its response within a single request, and that request is capped at 60 seconds. Structure prediction works differently. title: Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot
abstract: Speech-to-text inference is computationally intensive. Each audio file triggers a pipeline of deep learning models (acoustic models, language models, and post-processing stages) running on NVIDIA GPUs to meet latency requirements. At scale, this means thousands of GPU instances running continuously. AssemblyAI needed a way to run GPU-intensive inference workloads cost-effectively at scale, without sacrificing the availability and latency guarantees their customers depend on. Running entirely on On-Demand Instances would be cost-prohibitive. Spot Instances offer significant savings, while Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. AssemblyAI needed an architecture that absorbs Spot interruptions gracefully while maintaining service level agreement (SLA) commitments. Additionally, customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, finance, and legal, must keep audio data within specific geographic boundaries. They implement strict data residency configurations in European AWS Regions. Available on AWS Marketplace , AssemblyAI provides an API for transcription, speaker detection, sentiment analysis, chapter detection, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction. Their models transcribe and analyze speech for high-volume workloads across industries including technology, media, healthcare, and financial services. In this post, we show you how AssemblyAI runs cost-optimized AI inference at scale for their speech-to-text platform. The architecture uses Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Spot Instances, and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Together, these services combine a flexible fleet of NVIDIA GPUs, ECS capacity providers, and a queue-based retry mechanism. The result is significant cost savings while maintaining SLA commitments across European AWS Regions. Solution overview AssemblyAI’s inference platform runs on Amazon ECS with compute capacity managed through ECS capacity providers. The fleet mixes Amazon EC2 Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances across multiple NVIDIA GPU instance families, running a single inference model per GPU at a scale of thousands of instances. The architecture is built on four pillars that work together to deliver cost-optimized and resilient inference: Amazon ECS capacity providers mixing Spot and On-Demand. Multi-family GPU Spot diversification across EC2 instance types (such as g4dn.xlarge, g4dn.2xlarge, g5.xlarge, g5.4xlarge, and g6.2xlarge). Queue-based retry architecture using Amazon SQS for interruption recovery. Regional deployment across US West (Oregon) us-west-2 and Europe (London) eu-west-2 for data residency compliance. The following diagram illustrates how this solution is deployed: Figure 1: AssemblyAI’s inference architecture on Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 Spot GPU instances and an Amazon SQS-based retry mechanism An Amazon ECS cluster runs within a virtual private cloud (VPC) across multiple Availability Zones. The cluster hosts GPU-backed ECS tasks (shown as ECS Task, GPU Spot 1 and ECS Task GPU Spot 2) that poll the queue and process inference jobs. Each task retrieves audio files from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and writes the completed transcription to a results store, which AssemblyAI configures to deliver the output to the end customer. When a Spot Instance receives an interruption notice, Amazon EventBridge invokes the Spot Interruption Handler (an AWS Lambda function). The handler returns the in-flight job to the Main Job SQS Queue so another healthy ECS task can pick it up. Customers configure their system to route jobs that exhaust retry attempts to a Dead Letter SQS Queue for investigation. Amazon CloudWatch Metrics monitors the health of the fleet and the Spot interruption events, providing observability across the system. title: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Amazon Bedrock provides built-in, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it. The identity flows along with organizational tags, into AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) and AWS Cost Explorer while keeping data inside the AWS security boundary. This post shows you how to use these capabilities to answer three questions that every FinOps and AI Platform leader asks as AI tool adoption scales: What is the real per-user cost? Which teams generate the most spend, and does that spend correlate with the value they deliver? How should next year’s budget scale with headcount and adoption? The approach works identically regardless of which AI coding or productivity tool makes the call. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode all invoke Amazon Bedrock through one of two inference endpoints: bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle , and Bedrock’s attribution mechanism operates at the endpoint layer, beneath any tool-specific logic. You configure identity propagation once, and every tool that routes inference through Bedrock inherits per-user cost visibility automatically. By the end of this post, you will have AWS IAM Identity Center configured with your external identity provider for per-user attribution, session tags (team, cost center) flowing into CUR 2.0, Amazon Athena queries and dashboard options for ongoing cost visibility, and a clear understanding of Bedrock-native usage controls to enforce spending limits. How Amazon Bedrock attribution works Amazon Bedrock records the IAM identity of every inference caller with no changes required to your API calls. When a user invokes a model through either the bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle endpoint, Bedrock captures the caller’s full IAM ARN, including the session name for federated users and publishes it to CUR 2.0 in the line_item_iam_principal column. In billing data, usage is aggregated per principal and per usage type for each export interval: one hour in an hourly export, one day in a daily export. CUR does not contain per-request cost. For per-prompt detail, use model invocation logs or request metadata tagging. Optionally, you can attach tags to IAM principals or pass session tags during federation to add organizational dimensions. These tags appear in CUR 2.0 with the iamPrincipal/ prefix and in Cost Explorer as filterable dimensions. The mechanism supports four access patterns: IAM users, per-application roles, federated identities, and large language model (LLM) gateways proxying to Bedrock. For a comparison of all four, see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock . This post follows the federated identity pattern, which is the natural fit for AI coding and productivity tools where each developer or knowledge worker authenticates individually. Amazon Bedrock offers additional attribution mechanisms beyond IAM principal tracking that organizations can layer depending on their needs (see Appendix A for a comparison). With Application Inference Profiles, you can tag spend by workload on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. With Projects and Workspaces, you can isolate and tag spend on the bedrock-mantle endpoint. Per-request metadata tagging provides per-prompt token-level detail in model invocation logs for workloads that need granularity finer than finer than CUR 2.0’s per-usage-type aggregation per export interval. You can combine these, for example, IAM principal attribution for per-user dollars on your invoice alongside per-request metadata tags for per-prompt detail in logs. The choice depends on your goal (see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock ). The attribution problem The developer and productivity tools run on each user’s machine and call Amazon Bedrock directly, or through an LLM gateway. title: Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture
abstract: Foundation models deployed on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod meet inputs that no pre-curated dataset covers: domain-specific jargon, unexpected formats, new products, and changing user behavior. Without a record of production inference data, teams can’t detect drift, find failure patterns, or use real interactions to improve the model. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now provides Data Capture, a built-in capability that records live inference inputs and outputs to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at three independent tiers, with minimal latency impact and zero impact on model availability. In this post, we walk through one complete example on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster. A home-appliance support router captures its production traffic, Amazon Athena queries surface a new-product blind spot, a SQL policy labels the captured records, and a fine-tune on that data teaches the router the new product. We measure accuracy before and after, on data that could not have existed before the model was deployed. The inference operator serves the model on one node, and the training operator runs the fine-tuning on another. We use synthetic data for the walkthrough. The scripts, manifests, SQL, synthetic datasets, and expected outputs are available in the accompanying GitHub repository . Three-tier Data Capture architecture HyperPod Data Capture provides three independent tiers, each at a different point in the request path. You can turn on any combination in the same dataCapture block. Tier 1: SageMaker endpoint Tier 2: Load balancer Tier 3: Model pod What’s captured Full request/response payloads Application Load Balancer (ALB) access-log fields: request line, status codes, timings, client IP, user agent Full request/response payloads plus event metadata Managed by SageMaker native data capture ALB access logs HyperPod inference operator (NGINX + OTel collector + S3 uploader sidecars) Best for Compliance, Model Monitor, audit Traffic and error-rate monitoring at low cost Debugging, analytics, training-data collection Configuration sagemakerEndpoint: — sampling %, input/output, AWS KMS loadBalancer: { enabled: true } modelPod: — sampling %, input/output, buffer, max payload size, AWS KMS, content types Tiers 1 and 3 both store full payloads, so enabling both stores every record twice. Use Tier 1 for compliance and Model Monitor, Tier 2 when you only need traffic metadata, and Tier 3 when you intend to use the payloads. This post uses Tier 3 only. Because Tier 3 records complete payloads, which can include names, addresses, and order numbers, protect that data before it becomes training data. Use sampling, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption ( kmsKeyId ), S3 lifecycle rules, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction (for example, with Amazon Comprehend). Prerequisites A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), with the inference operator installed ( Setting up your HyperPod clusters for model deployment ) and the training operator EKS add-on amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-training-operator installed ( Installing the training operator ). Two available NVIDIA GPUs , one for serving and one for training. We used an ml.g6e.8xlarge for serving and an ml.g6e.xlarge for training (one 48 GB NVIDIA L40S each). The serving pod holds its GPU for the life of the endpoint, so with only one GPU the training pod stays Pending . kubectl configured for the cluster. An S3 bucket in the same Region. title: What Makes an Agent Self-Evolving?
abstract: An agent can get better at its job without a new model. It can learn to find useful information, choose the right tool, or check that a task is finished before reporting success. For that experience to help with the next task, something has to carry over: an updated instruction, a lesson saved in memory, or a change to the software that runs the agent. That is what interests me about a self-evolving agent: It can use experience to change how it handles future tasks. Much of that change happens in the harness , the instructions, context, tools, and software around the model. Research such as Harness-RSI explores how agents can change that harness while continuing to use the same model. Of course, a change can make things worse. A saved memory might be wrong, or a new instruction might fix one problem and create another. I think about self-evolving agents in three parts: evaluation to tell whether a change helped, an improvement process that can do more of the work on its own, and the parts of the harness it is allowed to change. Evaluation: What counts as improvement? Before I ask an agent to improve itself, I want to know what doing a better job would look like. A model’s score on a benchmark tells us how it performed on that test. To evaluate an agent built with that model, we also need to ask whether it used the right information, took the right actions, and met the user’s requirements. In a restaurant-planning exercise I developed for teaching evaluation, an agent is given a group’s needs and information about restaurants. Its job is to suggest a place and a time for dinner. The people and restaurants are fictional, but success is easy to understand: Can everyone eat there, afford it, and make it on time? In one test, the agent recommended a restaurant that met everyone’s needs. My evaluation still marked the answer as wrong because it compared the wording with a sample answer I had written. But my answer was only one possible solution. A different recommendation could work just as well. That feedback could lead a self-improving agent to “fix” a decision that was already good. A more useful evaluation would check whether the recommendation met the group’s requirements. If someone’s budget is $25 and the meal costs $28, the plan fails that check. We can build a custom evaluation around those requirements, checking the price, dietary needs, and timing. Other questions require judgment, such as whether the agent clearly explained a trade-off between price and convenience. A person or another model can help assess those. If we asked the agent to make a booking as well, we would need to check that the reservation actually existed. A message saying, “Your table is booked” would not be enough. Evaluating the system means checking what it did, as well as what it said. Once the agent proposes a change, we can test the updated version against the current one. It should still handle tasks it already did well. We should also try cases that were not used to develop or choose the change. Getting one dinner plan right tells us less than handling new groups with different budgets, dietary needs, and schedules. The evaluation should also explain why an answer failed. “The meal costs more than the guest’s budget” gives the agent something specific to investigate. It still needs to find the cause, but it knows where to start. Autonomous improvement: Who carries the work forward? If an engineer has to spot every failure, suggest every change, and start every test, improvement still depends on that person. Autonomous improvement means giving more of this work to the system. It can review past tasks, look for repeated mistakes, propose a change, and test whether the change helps. For example, a more autonomous dinner planner might notice that it repeatedly recommended restaurants people could not afford, even though their budgets were available. title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
abstract: This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings. Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms. Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my LLM gallery . But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis. Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover different positional methods in LLMs; (finally) how RoPE works; what methods are used by recent open LLMs. Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) . If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my self-attention walkthrough as a refresher: The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style. PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added image exports and metadata from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses. title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
abstract: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it . The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough . Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy. The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however. The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants. Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
abstract: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment. What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else. In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die. Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand. title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
abstract: Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics , governance , and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges. “AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance. Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union , the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology , and the International Organization for Standardization . The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias , security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap. Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies. Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust. Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance. The benefits of microcredentials Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program. Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment. For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles. Translating standards into microcredentials Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards , most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle. The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust. To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert .

title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
abstract: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry. The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military's national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday's mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX's Starlink. Sunday's failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time. Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights. Read full article Comments

title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
abstract: Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people's lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities. Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people's impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences. A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity. Read full article Comments

title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
abstract: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket. Read full article Comments

title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
abstract: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
abstract: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
abstract: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
abstract: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same. Read full article Comments

title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
abstract: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
abstract: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006). title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
abstract: How do you think you're going to die? If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident." In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said. Read full article Comments

title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
abstract: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates. title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
abstract: As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point. It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever. Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn't starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, "they will be squeezed to death," he wrote. Read full article Comments

title: Screenless GPS: Slate Auto says, "Remember the road atlas"
abstract: Whether it's nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch : an affordable electric truck with just the basics , leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price. Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it's called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review. That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now. title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
abstract: ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming. Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement . When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus. Read full article Comments

title: Specialized’s Tarmac SL9 S-Level is built to wreck your Zone 2 ride
abstract: I love a good Zone 2 ride . There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I'd count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding. The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don't need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. title: AI 시대의 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생 개발자에게
abstract: 시작하며: 2018년과 2026년 사이의 간격과 격변기의 고민 ​ 2018년에 저는 ' 백엔드 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생개발자에게 '라는 글을 이곳 D2 블로그에 공유했습니다. 당시 학생 개발자들과의 미트업 행사에서 나왔던 질문과 답변을 정리한 글이었습니다. 그 후 8년의 시간이 흘렀기에 그 글만 노출된다면 학생들에게 현시점에 적절한 정보를 주지 못할까 봐 걱정되었습니다. 그래서 2025년 말 설문으로 질문을 받아 후속편을 작성했습니다. ​ 그동안 저도 경험과 지식을 더 쌓았습니다. 하지만 지금 학생 개발자들이 한 질문에는 답하기가 더 어려워졌습니다. 개발자의 역할과 같은 큰 주제를 묻는 질문이 많았는데, 지금은 AI로 인한 변화가 큰 시기이기 때문입니다. 스스로도 확신이 없는 시기에 이런 글을 쓰는 것이 적절할지 고민도 했습니다. ​ 그럼에도 2018년의 글에 보내 주신 관심에 용기를 얻어서 이 글을 발행합니다. 최근의 경험을 나누고 미래를 함께 상상해 보는 일이 지금 시점에는 더 의미가 있다고 생각합니다. 이 글을 목적지가 명확한 안내서보다는 격변기의 스냅샷 정도로 봐 주셨으면 합니다. 주요 질문과 답변 설문을 통해 들어온 질문들을 비슷한 주제로 모아서 답변을 정리했습니다. [AI 시대와 개발자] 가장 비중이 높은 질문 유형이었고 근본적인 주제이기도 합니다. 이 질문에 먼저 답하지 않고서는 다른 이야기를 풀어 가기가 어려웠습니다. ​ ​ AI 시대에 개발자의 역할은 어떻게 달라졌을까요? 누군가는 AI를 인터넷이나 전기, 불에 비견될 정도의 혁명이라고 말합니다. [1] 2025년부터는 그 주장이 과장이 아니라고 느낍니다. 제가 프로그래밍을 시작한 1989년 이후로 '코딩’이라는 활동에 가장 큰 변화가 왔습니다. AI 코딩 도구가 코드를 추천해 주는 역할에서 나아가 소스 작성, OS 명령 실행 등 사람의 실질적인 대리로 행동합니다. ​ 역사를 돌아보면 기술이 발전하면서 지식 근로자가 하는 일은 이전 시대 관리자의 역할에 가까워졌습니다. 1980년대에 개인용 컴퓨터가 보급되기 전까지 지식 근로자의 작업 공간은 종이였고, 수기로 정보를 처리하는 일에 쓰는 시간의 비중이 컸습니다. AI 시대 전에도 계산, 정보의 형식 변환과 취합 등 컴퓨터가 하는 일의 범위는 꾸준히 늘어 왔습니다. 과거의 실무 일부를 컴퓨터가 하게 되면서 말단의 지식 근로자도 영향력이 큰 의사결정에 많이 관여할 수 있게 되었고 권한도 커졌습니다. ​ CAD 도입 전 General Motors의 기술자들이 작업하는 모습 (이미지 출처: ArchDaily ) 이제는 조직의 말단 작업자는 AI이고 모든 개발자는 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었습니다. 사람은 여러 AI 에이전트에게 업무를 지시하고 결과에 피드백을 줍니다. 아래에 나열한 일들은 전통적인 관리자의 역할이기도 하지만 '작업자’를 'AI 에이전트’로 바꿔서 읽어 본다면 이제는 모든 개발자가 하는 일입니다. ​ 다수의 작업자에게 목표와 배경, 추구하는 가치, 평가 기준을 제시한다. 작업자의 정보 탐색 비용을 줄여 준다. 참조할 정보가 어디에 있는지 알려 준다. 작업자별 역할을 명확히 정의하여 할 일을 분배한다. 작업자별 장점과 투자액(과금액) 수준을 고려하여 각자의 작업에 집중할 수 있도록, 컨텍스트가 과도하게 넓어지지 않고 컨텍스트 전환이 최소화되도록 의사결정자와 작업자 간의 효율적인 피드백 사이클을 구축한다. ​ 관리 업무의 멀티태스킹도 개발자가 적응해야 할 환경이 되었습니다. 에이전트에게 많은 일을 맡기려면 다수의 작업자가 병렬로 일을 진행할 수 있도록 지시를 내리고 결과물에는 빠른 피드백을 주어야 합니다. 작업자마다 컨텍스트를 좁혀 줄수록, 넓은 범위의 맥락을 머리에 올려 두고 빠르게 전환해야 하는 부담은 사람에게 더 크게 돌아옵니다. AI 에이전트와 일하는 형태는 여러 메신저 창을 왔다 갔다 하면서 다수와 병렬로 대화를 이어 가는 관리자의 모습과도 닮아 갑니다. 어떤 순간에는 화면을 어지럽게 전환하면서 게임 유닛에게 작업 지시와 확인, 판단을 쉴 틈 없이 하는 프로게이머와도 유사하게 느껴집니다. ​ 정보를 찾을 수 있는 연결 체계와 필요한 권한을 제공하여 에이전트가 막힘없이 일하도록 하는 일이 중요해지고 있습니다. 부작용을 줄이며 코드를 고치고 빠르게 피드백을 받을 수 있는 아키텍처와 워크플로를 설계하는 일도 핵심 업무가 됩니다. 개발자 경험(Developer Experience)뿐만이 아니라 AI 에이전트 입장에서 얼마나 일을 하기 쉬운지가 생산성을 좌우하게 됩니다. 이는 개발 리더가 다른 개발자들이 일하기 좋은 코드 구조와 작업 절차를 잡아 주는 일과도 유사합니다. 아키텍처와 기술 스택, 구현 방식 같은 기술 의사결정은 여전히 중요합니다. 합리적으로 결정하면 AI 에이전트가 더 안전하고 빠르게 일하고, 그렇지 못하면 오히려 기술부채를 쌓습니다. 예를 들면 모듈 경계가 분명하면 에이전트는 고칠 범위를 좁게 잡지만, 경계가 흐리면 비슷한 코드를 여기저기 복제합니다. ​ 더 상위 수준의 설계까지 AI가 맡는 다음 단계도 이미 시작되고 있습니다. 최근의 코딩 에이전트는 다른 에이전트에게 일을 분배하는 리더 역할까지도 수행합니다. 아키텍처도 AI가 제안하는 방향을 개발자가 수용하거나 근거로 드는 빈도가 높아지고 있습니다. 리더와 아키텍트 역할까지 AI가 가져간다면, 조직 수준의 투자와 리스크 감수를 결정하는 일이 사람의 역할로 남을 것입니다. 앞에서 모든 개발자가 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었다고 말씀드렸는데, 이 단계까지 가면 모든 회사 구성원이 한 번 더 승진을 하는 셈입니다. 조직도상의 개인 기여자도 일하는 형태로는 여러 실무팀의 리더들의 리더가 됩니다. 현실 세계 조직도상의 조직장은 리더들의 리더들의 리더가 되니, 적어도 소기업 경영진의 관점에서 생각하고 결정하는 빈도가 높아질 것 같습니다. 경영진이 투자 대비 사업 성과를 평가하듯, AI 사용료에서 종량제 비중이 높아지면서 한 번의 세션, 한 번의 프롬프트가 주는 부가가치에도 이전보다 신경을 쓰게 됩니다. ​ AI는 지치지 않고 병렬로 일하는 대신 세션이 끝나면 맥락을 잊습니다. 이처럼 사람과 지능의 성격이 다르니 관리하는 방법도 달라야 합니다. 그 차이를 전제하더라도, 관리자의 일하는 방식에 하나의 정답이 없다는 점은 AI와 일하는 방식을 고를 때도 참고가 됩니다. 개발을 모르는 팀장도 팀원들에게 맡기면 결과물은 나오고, 몰라서 더 많이 위임하기에 생기는 장점도 있습니다. 반면 개발을 잘 아는 팀장은 처음부터 올바른 방향을 지시해 시행착오를 줄이기도 합니다. ​ AI 에이전트와 일할 때도 코드를 아는 개발자는 상황에 따라 마이크로매니징과 큰 단위의 위임 중에서 고를 수 있습니다. 이렇게 현미경과 망원경을 오가면서 AI를 감독할 수 있다면 특성과 민감도가 다양한 작업을 안정적으로 수행할 수 있을 것입니다. 제가 아는 뛰어난 개발자 중에서는 수 시간 동안 에이전트가 실행할 업무 정의를 잘하시는 분도 있습니다. 프롬프트를 내린 후에 중간에 나오는 메시지를 하나하나 다 보시면서 에이전트가 일을 어긋나게 수행하는 순간을 바로 잡아내시는 분도 있습니다. ​ ​ AI에게 맡겨도 되는 부분과 개발자가 직접 해야 하는 부분이 있을까요? 실행 능력만 놓고 보면 이제는 AI가 개발자가 하는 대부분의 일을 할 수 있고, 더 잘하는 일도 많습니다. 아무리 AI가 발전해도 할 수 없는 일이 무엇일지를 생각해 보면 이 질문에 오래가는 답을 찾을 수 있습니다. 사람만이 '책임’을 질 수 있습니다. AI 에이전트가 모든 작업을 다 해 준다고 해도 그 소프트웨어를 사용자가 쓰게 하는 결정은 사람이 내립니다. 그로 인해 사용자에게 미친 영향의 책임은 AI에게 지시를 내리고 그 결과물을 최종 승인한 사람에게 돌아갑니다. AI 생성 이미지 ​ 누구나 코드를 만들 수 있게 된 시대에 '개발자’라는 명칭이 앞으로도 쓰인다면, 민감한 시스템의 운영 환경에 코드 배포를 승인하는 사람이라는 의미가 가장 크지 않을까 합니다. 그렇다면 문제를 알아보고 예방할 수 있다는 믿음을 주는 사람에게 그런 권한을 부여하고 '개발자’라고 부를 가능성이 높습니다. 그런 믿음을 주려면 코드의 동작 결과를 검증하고 보장하는 장치와
